For a second, get the whole "regulated/unregulated/militia" thing out of your mind. There is a more fundamental thing you need to understand about the document, which is that it is a document about the federal government. Its commands pertain to the creation of the federal government, and the limits thereof. Now, it also discusses, in certain places, the relationship between it and the government of the several states; however, in every single such instance, there is a very specific phrase that is used: "No State shall..." For example, "No State shall ...coin money; grant letters of marque and reprisal; enter into compacts without the consent of the congress; engage in war..." (See Art. I, § 10.) Accordingly, when the document does not explicitly use such language, it is not talking about obligations on state governments or the limits imposed on their general powers of regulation (reserved to them, of course, by default, but also explicitly confirmed through the 10th Amendment).

Look at the 5th amendment--specifically, the due process clause. Now look at the 14th amendment's due process clause. They have identical language, right? For the most part, they do. But if the 5th amendment already restricted states from depriving one of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, that same language in the 14th amendment would be entirely duplicative, and thus superfluous. We do not interpret the text of public law in ways that would render superfluous any word, phrase, etc.

Moreover, they are not entirely identical provisions. As you can see, the 14th amendment precedes its due process clause with those "magic words": "No State shall...deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law..."

Now look at the other "Bill of Rights" Amendment (for our purposes, 1st through 8th. No "magic words" in those, right? (Indeed, the 1st explicitly commands that "Congress shall make no law..."--but don't dwell on that right now, there is a very technical reason for that atypical variance in the language, and it actually is consistent with everything I am saying here.) Accordingly, the commands in the Bill of Rights are only applicable as against the federal government, not the states.

Now, let's go to the 2nd Amendment.

"A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed."

The first part (before "the right...") is entirely prefatory, and creates no legal rights or obligations. It is merely stating what was (and in many ways still is) considered to be obvious: that the security of a free state requires that it have some militia-type body to keep the peace. The remainder of the amendment is where the legal obligations trigger.

"the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed."

That is pretty darn absolute. It creates a right to "keep and bear" (meaning have, possess, etc.) "Arms" (meaning weapons). In fact, it prevents any federal government action that even infringes on that right, not just those that directly violate it.

Now we can go back to that first part of the amendment--not because it has any interpretive force vis-a-vis the second part, but because, when viewed in this proper manner, it finally makes perfect sense:

A well regulated militia is indeed necessary to the security lf a free state. And how are those state militias well regulated? By state law! That's how! State law is what is allowed to regulate the keeping and bearing of arms. Indeed, here's the reality that no one (the NRA, etc.) understands:

Because the 2nd amendment does not apply to the states, they are permitted to set any restrictions they want concerning firearms--from no restrictions at all to an outright ban, it is all up to each state to set their own policies. It does mean, however, that the federal government cannot constitutionally regulate on this subject.

Now, of course, this may be impractical in today's world, if only because federal control over an industry like firearms is important, and no state has the geographic authority or resources to effectively accomplish this. But all that means is that we must amend the Second Amendment to allow for this. In the meantime:

Federal laws restricting the possession/use of firearms (or weapons) of any kind: Unconstitutional.

Illinois gun-control laws (e.g., prohibition on concealed weapons): Constitutional.

Exact same gun-control laws (as Illinois, above), but for the District of Columbia (which is regulated by Congress): Unconstitutional

Hypothetical California law prohibiting the possession of all firearms of any kind, for any purpose: Constitutional (but that does not, in any way, equate with wise--it just means that they can do it).

So you can see how completely off-base virtually everyone participating in this debate has been. We're backwards right now--decrying state gun control laws as unconstitutional, while upholding challenges to federal gun control legislation (virtually without exception). We can't even properly delineate the scope of what our federal and state governments can do--in my view, we must be clear on that part before we take any action regarding what we ought to do. And that means we need to amend the f#@%ing Constitution first.
